name: Hungary 1950–56 (Golden Team)
scopeNote: Hungary national team (the Golden Team / Aranycsapat) under Gusztáv Sebes, from the start of the unbeaten run in June 1950 to the end of the era in 1956; period and manager kept from the earlier file. Day-level dates found but not applied (see openQuestions): the run began with Poland 2–5 Hungary in Warsaw on 4 June 1950 (Wikipedia results list; FIFA 2020 calls it '70 years ago today' on 3 June 2020), and Sebes's last match was Belgium 5–4 Hungary on 3 June 1956, after which he was sacked (en Wikipedia; hu Wikipedia says early July 1956). Key matches: Olympic gold 1952 (2–0 v Yugoslavia, 1952-08-02), Italy 0–3 in Rome (1953-05-17), England 3–6 at Wembley (1953-11-25), 7–1 v England (1954-05-23), World Cup 1954 runners-up (lost 3–2 to West Germany, 1954-07-04). Style: a WM variation built on a deep-lying centre-forward (Hidegkuti, 'false nine role' in TFT), a left-half (Zakariás) who dropped into the back line, attacking full-backs, inward wingers, constant rotation of the five forwards, and a sweeper-keeper (Grosics). Sebes's own term for it is 'socialist football' (FIFA, attributed). The shape label is disputed between sources: 3–2–3–2 (en Wikipedia), 2-3-3-2 (UEFA 2015), 'three full-backs and two half-backs' (TFT), 'a kind of 4-2-4' (hu Wikipedia; Buzánszky in UEFA 2003: 'his 4-2-4 tactics'), and 4-3-3 for the Rome 1953 match (Nemzeti Sport 2006). The common thread is a back three plus Zakariás dropping in, i.e. four defending, which is why later writers call it 4-2-4. Tactics were shaped with Márton Bukovi and Gyula Mándi on the staff; Wilson calls Bukovi the strongest claimant to be the 'mastermind'. Marking: no source says Hungary marked zonally; the period evidence (1953 match report ratings, FA Year Book 'the same defensive tactics') points to WM-style individual duties in defence.
openQuestions: Period kept as in the earlier file (1950-06 to 1956). Exact days found: start 1950-06-04 (Poland 2–5 Hungary, first match of the unbeaten run, Wikipedia results list; FIFA's 2020 article implies 3 June), end 1956-06-03 (Belgium 5–4 Hungary, Sebes's last match, en Wikipedia; hu Wikipedia says he was replaced in early July 1956). Decide whether to pin the period and managers[] to these days; the Soviet Union 0–1 Hungary win (1956-09-23) was under Bukovi and would fall outside a Sebes-only end.

Formation label: sources give 3–2–3–2, 2-3-3-2, 'three full-backs and two half-backs', 'a kind of 4-2-4' and 4-3-3 (Rome 1953). Decide whether this profile is the 4–2–4 exemplar (as the ideology file says) or a WM variation that later writers read as 4–2–4.

Marking (mar): the dedicated search (English and Hungarian) found no source that says Hungary's own defence was zonal or man-oriented. The evidence is indirect: period ratings of individual duels (Lantos v Matthews), the FA Year Book saying Hungary used 'the same defensive tactics' as the English style, and Lantos 'left Rahn free' at the corner in the 1954 final. The only 'zonal' claim found (FourFourTwo via Daily News Hungary) is about Lóránt as a coach in Germany years later, outside the period. A search summary also claimed a page called Hungary's marking zonal; it was not on the pages read (Sportskeeda, footballbh).

Who decided: Wilson (2025) says Bukovi, with no official role, has the best claim to be the mastermind and Sebes was 'by his own admission, no great tactician'; Buzánszky (2003) credits Sebes with putting the system together. The article body is paywalled, so Wilson's source for the admission was not seen.

No primary, dated Sebes statement about his football was found; every Sebes quote is attributed (FIFA 2012/2020, TFT 2020, Wikipedia) or a translated reprint (Nemzeti Sport 2006). Stated-view stays a gap.
Quotes from UEFA.com were read through the page reader (direct download fails): the wording was asked for verbatim but should be spot-checked.

Squad-building: the only source that says Sebes brought in young players (UEFA 2015: 'youthful, malleable fresh faces like Sándor Kocsis and Zoltán Czibor') describes 1949, before the period; in the period the evidence is of a fixed XI from two clubs (continuity, experience).

sources.title: Golden Team (Wikipedia)
sources.evidence: 'Key people': "Sebes's tactic was to withdraw the centre forward back to the midfield, as well as dropping the wingers back to the midfield when necessary. This effectively created an extremely flexible 3–2–3–2 formation". 'Historic significance': "the 3–2–3–2 eventually evolving into the 4–2–4 formation." Era-wide, no single date (dated 1953 as the system's best-known year).

sources.title: Gusztáv Sebes: the pioneering brain behind Hungary's Magical Magyars (These Football Times, Greg Lea)
sources.evidence: "As well as the use of a withdrawn centre-forward, Hungary innovated by employing three full-backs and two half-backs, a diversion from the more traditional WM formation which paired two full-backs with three half-backs. Zakarias regularly dropped back into defence, while Grosics was encouraged to leave his penalty area and sweep up behind the back line." Described for the 1953 side before Wembley.

sources.title: Gusztáv Sebes: the pioneering brain behind Hungary's Magical Magyars (These Football Times, Greg Lea)
sources.evidence: Central European Cup v Switzerland, "six weeks after the Olympic final": "With Hungary two goals down ... Sebes replaced Palotás with Hidegkuti in the false nine role. It worked a treat, and Hungary rarely deviated from the new arrangement thereafter."

sources.title: The Intellect Won instead of Strength in London (Nemzeti Sport Online)
sources.evidence: Italy 0–3 Hungary, Rome, 17 May 1953: "Before three defenders, Jenő Buzánszky, Gyula Lóránt, Mihály Lantos he put József Zakariás into the role of a moving player ... He ordered Nándor Hidegkuti back from the centre ... The arrangement applied then would be in accordance with the 4-3-3 system"; "it was a tactics considerably more defensive than the WM". Also: "The Hungarian national team also played in the WM system, officially at least." Hungarian national sports daily, retrospective analysis (2006).

sources.title: Aranycsapat (Hungarian Wikipedia)
sources.evidence: "Sebes Gusztáv szövetségi kapitány a Bukovi Márton által megkezdett úton továbbhaladva a csapat balfedezetét és középcsatárát is visszavontabban játszatta, és egyfajta 4-2-4-es hadrendet hozott létre. Az addig szokásos három védő helyett négyen védekeztek" (withdrew the left-half and the centre-forward, 'a kind of 4-2-4'; four defended instead of three). Era-wide.

sources.title: Wembley memories haunt Buzánszky (UEFA.com)
sources.evidence: Buzánszky (Hungary right-back at Wembley), interviewed 2003: "For Buzánszky, coach Gusztáv Sebes and his 4-2-4 tactics were the key to the victory." Buzánszky: "It was a very attack-minded team with five forwards." Read through the page reader (UEFA.com does not load by direct download).

sources.title: The greatest teams of all time: Hungary 1950–56 (UEFA.com)
sources.evidence: "Sebes pioneered a radical variation of the WM formation, featuring a withdrawn centre-forward and wingers who could slot into midfield when required, to create a flexible 2-3-3-2 lineup." Read through the page reader.

sources.title: Match of the Century (1953 England v Hungary football match) (Wikipedia)
sources.evidence: "The Hungarian team lined up in the 3–2–3–2 formation pioneered by their coach, Gusztáv Sebes. József Bozsik played in the deep-lying midfield position, with Nándor Hidegkuti free to roam between midfield and attack. Ferenc Puskás and Sándor Kocsis were the strikers, with the width provided by Zoltán Czibor and László Budai."

sources.title: Gusztáv Sebes: the pioneering brain behind Hungary's Magical Magyars (These Football Times, Greg Lea)
sources.evidence: Hidegkuti, undated: "Though all six of us [Bozsik, Czibor, Budai, Puskás, Kocsis and himself] could attack, we never played in a line formation ... If I went forward, Puskás dropped back. If Kocsis drifted wide, Bozsik moved into middle. ... we constantly changed positions, so where we lined up at kick-off was irrelevant." Player quote with no date given.

sources.title: Gusztáv Sebes: the pioneering brain behind Hungary's Magical Magyars (These Football Times, Greg Lea)
sources.evidence: "Grosics was encouraged to leave his penalty area and sweep up behind the back line. When the ball was in his possession, Puskás and Hidegkuti moved towards rather than away from their goalkeeper – the exact opposite of what was commonplace at the time."

sources.title: Hungary's unsung hero of 6:3 legend (LiberoGuide, Peterjon Cresswell)
sources.evidence: Wembley: "In the dressing room at Wembley, Sebes stressed to his No.6 his defensive role in front of the back three, allowing Bozsik to roam and create. Barely 45 seconds had gone when Zakariás played a short pass to Bozsik, who fed Hidegkuti to strike from the edge of the box." Draws on István Szeidl's Zakariás biography (2002).

sources.title: Match of the Century (1953 England v Hungary football match) (Wikipedia)
sources.evidence: "England were simply unable to obtain the ball"; "Hungary had 35 shots on goal to England's five and their final goal, a Hidegkuti volley, followed a ten-pass sequence." Period quote carried on the page (The Guardian report): "none of the English forwards except Matthews approached the speed, ball control, and positional play of the Hungarians".

sources.title: England v Hungary 1953 line-ups and FA Year Book report (RSSSF, rec.sport.soccer compilation)
sources.evidence: FA Year Book report of the match (period text, reproduced on RSSSF): the Hungarians "largely owed their victory to their mastering of the 'English Style' - interchanging forwards, a mingling of short and long passes, the same defensive tactics, but all performed with almost geometrical accuracy and ball control amounting to elegance"; "shot four of their six goals from outside the penalty area."

sources.title: Gold gives birth to the Magical Magyars (FIFA.com)
sources.evidence: Olympic final v Yugoslavia, Helsinki: "Hungary dominated possession from the outset, with Bozsik tormenting Yugoslavia with his piercing through-balls, Hidegkuti frustrating them with his elusive movement".

sources.title: The Intellect Won instead of Strength in London (Nemzeti Sport Online)
sources.evidence: Some Hungarian coaches, "e.g. Márton Bukovi, Gusztáv Sebes, considered necessary to reduce rigidity: to bring playing with many movements, short passes, changing positions, speed, but either not without long passes embracing the field."

sources.title: We scored six to England (Nemzeti Sport Online, reprint of the 1953 report plus Grosics and Buzánszky recollections)
sources.evidence: Grosics on England's second goal (recollection, 2006): "The host outside left, Robb held the ball, and we, instead of attacking him, drew back. Of course, Robb could calmly pass the ball to Mortensen". One match moment, a player's memory 53 years on.

sources.title: Gyula Grosics (Wikipedia)
sources.evidence: Grosics's sweeper-keeper style "allowed his teammates to press deep in their opponents' half". General claim, no match or date, no source quoted.

sources.title: We scored six to England (Nemzeti Sport Online, reprint of the 1953 report plus Grosics and Buzánszky recollections)
sources.evidence: Player ratings from the 1953 Hungarian report the page says it republishes ("we published it 53 years ago"), in English translation: Buzánszky "almost totally made his opponent disappear from the ground"; Lantos "had rather hard task against the technically well-trained and well-dribbling Stanley Matthews, he managed, however, his task, since he was the winner in most of the dogfights"; Lóránt "stopped several host attacks by excellent positioning ... he proved to be dominant in the space". Reads as full-backs given direct duels with the opposing wingers (left-back Lantos v outside-right Matthews), i.e. WM-style man-oriented duties on the flanks; the page does not use the words zonal or man-marking.

sources.title: England v Hungary 1953 line-ups and FA Year Book report (RSSSF, rec.sport.soccer compilation)
sources.evidence: FA Year Book (period): the Hungarians played "the same defensive tactics" as the 'English Style'. England were playing the WM, whose centre-half marked the centre-forward (see the Match of the Century page). Evidence that the Hungarian defence was organised like a WM defence, not that it was zonal.

sources.title: The Intellect Won instead of Strength in London (Nemzeti Sport Online)
sources.evidence: 1954 final: "after a German corner shot, Mihály Lantos left Rahn free to equalize (2:2)"; also "József Zakariás performed a poor pass to our goalkeeper and Morlock pitilessly exploited it". Assigning the goal to one defender who left one attacker free suggests individual marking at set pieces.

sources.title: Gusztáv Sebes: the pioneering brain behind Hungary's Magical Magyars (These Football Times, Greg Lea)
sources.evidence: Wembley: "Hidegkuti's between-the-lines positioning, Grosics' proactive goalkeeping, Bozsik's forwards runs from midfield and Zakarias' retreats into the defence all moves to which the hosts had no answer."

sources.title: Golden Team (Wikipedia)
sources.evidence: "previously, each player in a team was assigned a specific position or role, usually marking a specific opposition player. The Hungarian tactic of players constantly changing roles and positions could only be introduced by using a core set of talented players". Describes the attack's rotation; it does not say Hungary's defence stopped marking individually.

sources.title: The Magical Magyars (Guide to Football, tactical history)
sources.evidence: "The whole team played a more flexible game than the W-M sides it faced, and the contrast was clearest when it came up against teams still playing strict man-to-man marking." About the opponents' marking, not Hungary's own.

sources.title: The beginning of the Magyars' magic (FIFA.com)
sources.evidence: Puskás, undated: "When we attacked, everyone attacked," said Puskas, "and in defence it was the same." Retrospective quote, no date.

sources.title: Gusztáv Sebes: the pioneering brain behind Hungary's Magical Magyars (These Football Times, Greg Lea)
sources.evidence: Puskás, undated: "Instead of the magic square of half-backs and inside-forwards playing themselves into a state of exhaustion, it was decided the work should be shared out amongst the team ... Attack and defence should work harmoniously as one."

sources.title: Golden Team (Wikipedia)
sources.evidence: Scotland 2–4 Hungary, Hampden Park, 8 Dec 1954: Scotland pressed forward late but "were caught on a counter break right at the end of the match when Kocsis scored". The page heads the section '1955' but dates the match 8 December 1954.

sources.title: The Magical Magyars (Guide to Football, tactical history)
sources.evidence: "The wingers tucked in to support the inside forwards."

sources.title: Aranycsapat (Hungarian Wikipedia)
sources.evidence: "a szélekről pedig Budai László és Czibor Zoltán támogatták az összekötőket" (from the flanks Budai and Czibor supported the inside forwards).

sources.title: Gusztáv Sebes: the pioneering brain behind Hungary's Magical Magyars (These Football Times, Greg Lea)
sources.evidence: Puskás's goal at Wembley: "the most interesting element of the move is that Czibor, the outside left, provided the assist via a cut-back from the right flank."

sources.title: We scored six to England (Nemzeti Sport Online, reprint of the 1953 report plus Grosics and Buzánszky recollections)
sources.evidence: 1953 report: Budai "was quick; he dribbled inscrutably, his centrings brought the others arriving at the centre usually in position. He kept energy also for defence." Buzánszky (2006): "We did not have fix positions, so this is why it could happen that two players originally playing on the left side scored the goal on the right wing."

sources.title: Wembley memories haunt Buzánszky (UEFA.com)
sources.evidence: Buzánszky described as "the forward-thinking right-back of Hungary's Golden Squad, a defender who unsettled opposing teams with his forward forays". Article text, read through the page reader.

sources.title: Golden Team (Wikipedia)
sources.evidence: Scotland 2–4 Hungary: "Partick Thistle winger John Mackenzie constantly beating Hungary full back Mihály Lantos".

sources.title: We scored six to England (Nemzeti Sport Online, reprint of the 1953 report plus Grosics and Buzánszky recollections)
sources.evidence: Buzánszky on the fourth goal: "We got free kick from about 25 meters from the English goal. Puskás, while moving crosswise in front of the goal, put his foot to the right-footed bomb of Bozsik". The FA Year Book report (RSSSF) also has Puskás diverting "a free-kick by Boszik". One goal; no evidence of a rehearsed routine.

sources.title: Gusztáv Sebes: the pioneering brain behind Hungary's Magical Magyars (These Football Times, Greg Lea)
sources.evidence: Brazil 2–4 Hungary: "Lantos made no mistake from 12 yards on the hour mark." Full-back as penalty taker; one match.

sources.title: Gusztáv Sebes: the pioneering brain behind Hungary's Magical Magyars (These Football Times, Greg Lea)
sources.evidence: "Ahead of international fixtures, Sebes would routinely organise warm-up games against local club sides and instruct them to adopt the tactics of their upcoming opponents." Described as routine during his tenure; no single date.

sources.title: Gusztáv Sebes: the pioneering brain behind Hungary's Magical Magyars (These Football Times, Greg Lea)
sources.evidence: Before Wembley: "Hungary began playing with the heavier type of ball that was used in England at the time, while training camps were held near Lake Balaton ... Before the game Sebes held a four-hour-long tactical team talk".

sources.title: Gusztáv Sebes: the pioneering brain behind Hungary's Magical Magyars (These Football Times, Greg Lea)
sources.evidence: World Cup semi-final v Uruguay: "Sebes opted to deploy Palotás as his deep-lying centre-forward, with Hidegkuti moving to outside left." After the final Sebes was criticised "for dropping Budai; for selecting Tóth on the left and Czibor on the right; for overcomplicating matters and attempting to surprise West Germany, rather than sticking with the Plan A".

sources.title: The Intellect Won instead of Strength in London (Nemzeti Sport Online)
sources.evidence: Contrary reading of the final: "the Hungarian team didn't change tactics, but changed its composition. Instead of II László Budai, Mihály Tóth got into the beginning team. As he was a left wing forward, Zoltán Czibor got a position on the right side."

sources.title: Gusztáv Sebes: the pioneering brain behind Hungary's Magical Magyars (These Football Times, Greg Lea)
sources.evidence: Players adjusted the plan in-game: Buzánszky said Puskás, Hidegkuti and Bozsik, "our computers", "would routinely read the pattern of the game in the opening 15 minutes, deciphering the opposition's weaknesses and then devising a strategy to exploit them."

sources.title: Wembley memories haunt Buzánszky (UEFA.com)
sources.evidence: Buzánszky: "The role of the coach ends at the moment the whistle goes to start the game"; "you talk about tactics in the dressing-room"; "You have to have a captain like Puskás who can say, 'OK, the tactic isn't working - let's play like this'." On Sebes's part: "He had a decisive role in putting it together ... It was like arranging cogs in a wheel - everything had to fit." Read through the page reader.

sources.title: The greatest teams of all time: Hungary 1950–56 (UEFA.com)
sources.evidence: "Tactical discussions were regular, lengthy and usually included input from captain Puskás and other world-class players at the coaches' disposal." Read through the page reader.

sources.title: The Greatest Tactician in History - Part 1 (Jonathan Wilson, Wilson's World substack)
sources.evidence: Free preview only (rest paywalled): Bukovi "has a claim to have been the mastermind of the Aranycsapat ... But he was not the coach, nor did he have any official role ... so the manager's job went to Gusztav Sebes, a fine former player and an adept politician and organiser but, by his own admission, no great tactician." Wilson's paraphrase of an undated Sebes admission, no quote or date: not counted as a stated view.

sources.title: Gusztáv Sebes: the pioneering brain behind Hungary's Magical Magyars (These Football Times, Greg Lea)
sources.evidence: Staff: Sebes's staff "included Bukovi and Gyula Mándi"; "Sebes fostered a spirit of collaboration, and he certainly wasn't afraid to take on board the ideas of those he worked with; Bukovi and Mándi, for instance, were much more than mere yes-men."

sources.title: Golden Team (Wikipedia)
sources.evidence: "Sebes encouraged his players to be versatile – the ideal would be for any of his players to be able to play in any position." 'Historic significance': "Sebes also demanded rigorous training and standards of physical fitness from his players, as well as good tactic awareness ... the Hungarian side were able to outrun, outpass and outplay their opposition."

sources.title: Gusztáv Sebes: the pioneering brain behind Hungary's Magical Magyars (These Football Times, Greg Lea)
sources.evidence: Stanley Matthews (England right-winger at Wembley), autobiography: "Hungary were combining two styles – the British all-running cut and thrust and the short passing game of probing infiltration ... an imaginative combination of exacting ball control, speed of movement and esoteric vision". Opponent's view, written later.

sources.title: The beginning of the Magyars' magic (FIFA.com)
sources.evidence: Sebes on Kocsis, undated: "There has never been anybody better with his head ... But he was also a very complete striker who held the ball up and could finish with both feet." Puskás on Hidegkuti: "He was perfect for the role, sitting at the front of the midfield, making telling passes, dragging the opposition defence out of shape".

sources.title: Gusztáv Sebes: the pioneering brain behind Hungary's Magical Magyars (These Football Times, Greg Lea)
sources.evidence: Fitness: "He introduced frequent swimming sessions into Hungary's training regime to increase players' lung power." 1954 semi-final: "It was Hungary's superior fitness that allowed them to wrestle back the momentum in the additional half-hour".

sources.title: Gusztáv Sebes: the pioneering brain behind Hungary's Magical Magyars (These Football Times, Greg Lea)
sources.evidence: "By now, Hungary's first-choice starting XI was well established: Grosics, Jenő Buzánszky, Gyula Lóránt, Mihály Lantos, József Bozsik, József Zakarias, László Budai, Hidegkuti, Zoltán Czibor, Sándor Kocsis and Puskás." Club core: Honvéd and MTK "would supply the vast majority of the national team's players"; Sebes and staff "set up a nationwide scouting network".

sources.title: Golden Team (Wikipedia)
sources.evidence: "Sebes's idea of using a core set of players, drawn from just a handful of clubs ... By using players who were familiar with each other's strengths at a club level, Sebes introduced a sense of continuity at a national level". The same XI kept for years: continuity over renewal.

sources.title: The greatest teams of all time: Hungary 1950–56 (UEFA.com)
sources.evidence: "Recently appointed coach Gusztáv Sebes did away with the established stars"; "in came youthful, malleable fresh faces like Sándor Kocsis and Zoltán Czibor." Describes 1949, before the profile period (June 1950): context for how the squad was formed, not counted. Read through the page reader.

sources.title: Hungary's unsung hero of 6:3 legend (LiberoGuide, Peterjon Cresswell)
sources.evidence: "While tacticians such as Márton Bukovi introduced concepts such as 4-2-4 and the deep-lying centre-forward, Sebes oversaw the development of the national squad, arranging fixtures and bedding in younger players." No names or dates for the younger players.

sources.title: Gusztáv Sebes: the pioneering brain behind Hungary's Magical Magyars (These Football Times, Greg Lea)
sources.evidence: "Medical experts were brought in to explain the negative effects of cigarettes and alcohol. Instead of drinking sessions, the squad visited museums and art galleries, while trips to factories across the country were viewed favourably by the powers that be." Grosics, undated: Sebes "made a political issue of every important match or competition".

sources.title: We scored six to England (Nemzeti Sport Online, reprint of the 1953 report plus Grosics and Buzánszky recollections)
sources.evidence: György Szepesi (radio commentator on the 1953 trip), recollection: "Gusztáv Sebes brought rather strict timetable, but let off one of the breakfasts, and the team could have a coffee or tea break instead of it."

sources.title: Gusztáv Sebes: the pioneering brain behind Hungary's Magical Magyars (These Football Times, Greg Lea)
sources.evidence: World Cup final: Sebes was criticised "for flying the players' families over but forbidding them to see their loved ones until after the final".

sources.title: The greatest teams of all time: Hungary 1950–56 (UEFA.com)
sources.evidence: "Sebes, a former trade union organiser in Budapest and Paris, was undoubtedly the leader"; Grosics: "Sebes was very committed to socialist ideology." Read through the page reader.

sources.title: Hungary's unsung hero of 6:3 legend (LiberoGuide, Peterjon Cresswell)
sources.evidence: "Many speak of Sebes' reliance on the collective when trying to explain the reasons behind Hungary's international dominance from 1950 onwards, while others point to their finely honed technique."

statedView.note: FIFA: Sebes "famously described their intricate, cohesive style of play as 'socialist football'". No date or original source for the phrase; earliest appearance found is this page.

statedView.quote: There were some great sides around at the time – Soviet Union, Austria, Sweden, Yugoslavia, Italy – but I felt we had the players and tactics to compete with anyone
statedView.note: About the 1952 Olympics; undated recollection, English only.

statedView.quote: We had done what we had to do, and we had done it in style.
statedView.note: After the 1952 Olympic final ('said Sebes afterwards'); no original source. Result and style together.

statedView.quote: The bitter struggle between capitalism and communism is fought out not only between our societies, but also on the pitch.
statedView.note: Undated ('As the man himself once said'); Grosics confirms Sebes 'often said' this (same page, and UEFA 2015). Politics, not tactics.

statedView.quote: The Hungarian team surpassed its form until now and is worthy of the trust of its folks.
statedView.note: Post-Wembley 1953 remark in the 'coaches' opinion' box of the 1953 Hungarian report that Nemzeti Sport says it republished in 2006, in English translation; the 1953 original was not seen, so not primary.

statedView.quote: We played football as Jimmy Hogan taught us. When our football history is told, his name should be written in gold letters
statedView.note: Wikipedia, no date or source given; date is the access date, the earliest appearance was not traced.

influences.note: Sebes 'was inspired by the Austrian Wunderteam' and drew the national side from one or two clubs as Meisl had (en Wikipedia, TFT). Jimmy Hogan (no catalog id) is credited by Sebes and Barcs.

confidence.reason: One tier B article (TFT 2020) and many tier C sources (Wikipedia en/hu, UEFA, FIFA, Nemzeti Sport, Guide to Football), mostly retrospective; some period text (the 1953 FA Year Book report, the 1953 Hungarian match ratings as reprinted, The Guardian quote). Sources agree on the deep-lying centre-forward, the rotation and the sweeper-keeper but disagree on the formation label; marking is only inferred; no primary Sebes statement.
